name: Abbas the Great
info: Abbas I, fifth Safavid shah of Iran, born in Herat in 1571, broke the power of the Qizilbash with a slave-soldier corps, reconquered lost provinces from the Ottomans and Uzbeks, and made Isfahan his capital.

facts.born: 27 January 1571 in Herat, Khorasan; third son of Mohammad Khodabanda and Khayr al-Nisa Begum, of the Safavid dynasty
facts.died: 19 January 1629 at his palace in Farahabad on the Caspian coast; buried in Kashan
facts.role: Fifth Safavid shah of Iran, titular governor of Herat as a child, shah until his death in 1629
facts.known: the ghulam corps and the new standing army; the defeat of the Uzbeks and the Ottomans and the reconquest of lost provinces; the deportations and massacres in Georgia and Armenia; the capture of Hormuz with English help; the new capital at Isfahan; embassies to Europe; the killing and blinding of his sons

t: Abbas came to the throne of a divided Iran, its provinces held in part by the Ottomans and the Uzbeks and its court ruled by quarrelling Qizilbash factions, and he went on to rule it at its military, political and economic height.

He weakened the Qizilbash with a standing army and civil service of Georgian, Circassian and Armenian slave-soldiers, the ghulams, and with it retook Khorasan, the Caucasus and Mesopotamia, while his armies killed and deported tens of thousands in Georgia.

He moved the capital to Isfahan and rebuilt it, yet in his last years he had one son killed and two others blinded, and the Cambridge History of Iran blames the practice for the poor statesmanship of later shahs.
dyk: Abbas shaved off his beard at nineteen, keeping only his moustache, and so set a fashion in Iran; when an Ottoman ambassador made arrogant demands, he had the man's beard shaved and sent to the sultan.
ev: Abbas is born in Herat, the third son of Mohammad Khodabanda, governor of Khorasan
He has Murshid Qoli Khan, who had put him on the throne, killed after a banquet and rules in his own right
The Treaty of Constantinople cedes Azerbaijan, Shirvan, Dagestan and Tabriz, among other lands, to the Ottomans
He defeats the Uzbeks near Herat and moves his capital from Qazvin to Isfahan
The Iranians win a decisive victory over the Ottomans at Sufiyan, near Tabriz
Abbas has his eldest son, Mohammad Baqer Mirza, murdered at Rasht
With four English ships he retakes Hormuz from the Portuguese and takes Kandahar from the Mughals
Abbas dies at Farahabad; his grandson succeeds him as Shah Safi

sections.early:
Abbas was born on 27 January 1571 in Herat, the third son of Mohammad Khodabanda, governor of Khorasan, and Khayr al-Nisa Begum, daughter of a local ruler of Mazandaran. His grandfather was Tahmasp I, the second Safavid shah. His father, almost blind from an eye disease, was passed over for the succession. When Abbas was barely eighteen months old his parents were sent to Shiraz and he was made nominal governor of Herat, with the Ustajlu amir Shah Qoli Sultan as his guardian. He never saw his mother again and saw his father only fifteen years later. He learnt soldiering from his Qizilbash guardians, played polo and hunted, and was educated beside household slaves, probably Georgians, Armenians or Circassians.

Tahmasp I died on 14 May 1576 without naming an heir, and civil war followed. Haydar Mirza was proclaimed shah and killed at once. Ismail II, freed after twenty years in prison, murdered much of the Ustajlu tribe, including Abbas's guardian, and in November 1577 sent a man to Herat to kill the boy. The man delayed, citing the holy days, and Ismail died of poisoned opium on 24 November 1577.
sections.rise:
Mohammad Khodabanda was chosen shah in 1578 but proved weak, and his wife Khayr al-Nisa Begum took charge of government, even of campaigns. When she tried to dictate strategy against the Ottomans, the Qizilbash stormed the harem and strangled her on 26 July 1579. The murder made a deep impression on Abbas, which probably led to his belief that the Qizilbash had to be broken. In 1581 the governor Ali-Qoli Khan Shamlu proclaimed the ten-year-old Abbas shah in Khorasan as a figurehead of a rebellion, but the quarrel was settled. Abbas's brother Hamza Mirza, the crown prince, was assassinated in December 1586.

Murshid Qoli Khan Ustajlu then took Abbas from Ali-Qoli Khan and, with an Uzbek army besieging Herat, rode with him towards Qazvin along the Silk Road, gathering Qizilbash amirs until the escort numbered 2,000. Mohammad Khodabanda abdicated, and Abbas was crowned in Qazvin on 1 October 1587. Murshid Qoli Khan became vakil (viceroy) and began to confine the young shah to the palace. Abbas executed three of his mother's killers and exiled four more, and on 23 July 1589 he had Murshid killed after a banquet by four Qizilbash leaders. He then made a peace with the Ottomans in 1590 that gave up Tabriz, Azerbaijan, Shirvan, Dagestan and other lands.
sections.deeds:
Abbas used the ghulams, slave-soldiers brought mainly from Georgia, Circassia and Armenia, to offset the Qizilbash. He raised a force funded entirely by the crown, put ghulams in place of Qizilbash provincial governors and sent their revenues to the royal treasury. The new army had cavalry, musketeers, artillery and a bodyguard, about 40,000 men loyal to the shah, and he could field 500 cannon in a battle. The English brothers Anthony and Robert Shirley, who arrived in 1598, advised on its reorganisation.

With this army he attacked the Uzbeks in April 1598, defeated them near Herat on 9 August and held most of Khorasan, though Balkh was lost in 1602. He moved the capital to Isfahan in 1598. Against the Ottomans he retook Tabriz, took Yerevan in June 1604 and won at Sufiyan in 1605. In 1618 he ambushed an Ottoman army of 100,000 near Ardabil with 40,000 men, and in 1623 he seized Baghdad. In 1602 his forces expelled the Portuguese from Bahrain, and in 1622 he took Hormuz with four English ships, founding Bandar Abbas. Isfahan was rebuilt with mosques, baths, colleges and caravanserais, and painters such as Reza Abbasi worked in his studios. Silk production became a crown monopoly.
sections.opponents:
Abbas's rule in the Caucasus was marked by deportation and killing. By estimate, 130,000 to 200,000 Georgians, tens of thousands of Circassians and around 300,000 Armenians were deported to Iran during his reign. In 1614 he deported 30,000 Kakhetian peasants after the Georgian kings Luarsab II and Teimuraz I defected. A punitive expedition then killed perhaps 60,000 to 70,000 or 100,000 Georgians, with twice as many deported, removing about two thirds of Kakheti's population. He executed Luarsab in 1622 and had Teimuraz's mother Ketevan tortured to death in 1624 when she refused to renounce Christianity. His plan to deport or exterminate eastern Georgia's Christians has been described as genocidal. From 1604 his scorched-earth policy in Armenia resettled up to 300,000 Armenians, and thousands died on the way to Isfahan.

Of his own family, he had his son Mohammad Baqer Mirza murdered in 1615 after rumours of a plot, then grieved. In 1621 he blinded another son, Mohammad, for celebrating his accession during Abbas's illness, and in 1627 he partially blinded the third, Imam Qoli Mirza. Michael Axworthy called him a talented administrator and a ruthless autocrat with a dark twist of suspicion and brutality, and Donald Rayfield called him a murderous paranoiac when aroused. The Cambridge History of Iran blames the practice of eliminating princes for the lack of competent successors.
sections.last:
Abbas fell seriously ill in 1621, and his health was poor from then on. He recovered, but the illness was followed by his punishment of his son Mohammad, who was blinded and imprisoned in Alamut Castle after a plot to smuggle him to the Mughals was betrayed. In 1627 he had his last son, Imam Qoli Mirza, partially blinded and imprisoned in Alamut as well, for reasons that remain unclear.

Having shut out his own sons, Abbas chose as his heir Sam Mirza, the son of the murdered Mohammad Baqer Mirza, who was said to loathe his grandfather because of his father's death. He also faced continuing Georgian resistance: after Giorgi Saakadze defected in 1625 and led a new rebellion, Abbas won the subsequent war but lost half his army and had to accept Kartli and Kakheti as vassal states, abandoning his plans to eliminate Christians from the area. A further rebellion in 1626 cleared Iranian forces from most of the region, and the Georgian territories kept resisting until his death.

He died at his palace in Farahabad on the Caspian coast in 1629 and was buried in Kashan. Sam Mirza succeeded him at the age of 17 as Shah Safi. In 1638 the Ottomans retook Baghdad.
sections.legacy:
Abbas regained most of the lands lost by his predecessors and left a centralised monarchy with a regular army answerable to the shah, in place of a state held together by Qizilbash tribes. The Iranian–Ottoman frontier was finalised after his death at roughly the present Iran–Turkey and Iran–Iraq borders. The ghulam class he enlarged went on to play a crucial role for the rest of the Safavid era and later, until the end of the Qajar era. Isfahan, with the Masjed-e Shah, the Masjed-e Sheykh Lotfollah, the Ali Qapu, the Chehel Sotoun and the Naqsh-e Jahan Square, became the centre of Safavid architecture. His embassies began lasting contacts with Europe, and Persian fashions, such as men's shoes with heels, were adopted by European aristocrats.

Historians have judged him differently. Roger Savory called him the chief architect of the modern Iranian state, a brilliant strategist whose chief characteristic was prudence, who preferred diplomacy to war. Axworthy and Rayfield stress the ruthlessness and suspicion. The Cambridge History of Iran rejects the view that his death began the Safavid decline, since Iran continued to prosper through the seventeenth century, but holds that his treatment of princes weakened the later shahs. Stories of his wisdom and fairness entered Persian folklore, and the Turkmen poet Magtymguly, a century later, praised his eloquence.

summary: Abbas I (1571–1629) took the Safavid throne in a divided Iran and ended the Qizilbash hold on the army with ghulam slave-soldiers. He retook provinces from the Uzbeks and Ottomans, rebuilt Isfahan as his capital, and ruled Georgia and Armenia by massacre and deportation, while killing and blinding his own sons.
references: Sussan Babaie, Slaves of the Shah: New Elites of Safavid Iran (I.B. Tauris, 2004)
David Blow, Shah Abbas: The Ruthless King Who Became an Iranian Legend (I. B. Tauris, 2009)
Houchang Nahavandi, Shah Abbas, Empereur de Perse: 1587–1629 (Perrin, 1998)
notes: Accession date: the lede says he ruled 1588 to 1629 and that he was 16 when placed on the throne; the body gives Ramadan 1586 for the ride, late September 1587 for the entry into Qazvin and 1 October 1587 for the coronation, aged seventeen. I gave 1 October 1587 in the text where the body does, left the start of the reign out of facts.role and left out his age at accession. Editor to decide.
Isfahan: the article says he moved the capital there in 1598 (twice) but also says after defeating the Uzbeks; the Uzbek war had run to 1603. 1598 used.
The 130,000-200,000 / 300,000 deportation figures are 'estimated' in the article.
Kakheti dead: 'perhaps 60,000-70,000 or 100,000', both given. Armenian resettlement 'up to 300,000' under the scorched-earth policy and 'around 300,000' in the general estimate; both used.

Heir confusion: the article names the son blinded in 1621 as 'his heir, Mohammad Khodabanda' (the shah's father's name), while the family list calls him Soltan Mohammad Mirza (born 1591). I called him Mohammad. The article says he was later murdered by Shah Safi.

Mohammad Baqer: the lede says he was caught in a court intrigue involving leading Circassians; the death section says rumours of a plot with Farhad Beg Cherkes and the boar episode. Text follows the death section; the family list gives killed 25 January 1615.

Left out: the article's praise-heavy lines ('keen economic and commercial understanding', 'prosperity'), the paragraph on character (shaved beard kept in dyk only), the Treaty of Nasuh Pasha 1612 and the Kabardino-Balkaria claim, Mughal embassy details, the consorts and children lists, the quotation of Abbas on Christians, and the Shakespeare reference.
Ottoman war dates: the article calls it the 1603-1618 war; the Sufiyan victory 6 November 1605. Baghdad taken 1623, lost 1638 after his death.
Mohammad Baqer is born 1587 per the article; one sentence says Abbas's 'five sons' of whom three survived childhood; the list has more sons than five. Left out.

References left empty for the editor; the article's Bibliography holds Encyclopaedia Iranica entries (Savory, 'Abbas I') and Further reading lists Canby (ed.), Shah Abbas: The Remaking of Iran (British Museum Press, 2009), Bomati and Nahavandi, and Matthee, Persia in Crisis.
